content_text: [1/14 @MapleLeafCap] I analyzed 10,000+ buyside analyst reports from top hedge funds: - Found 7 things that separate great stock pitches from mediocre ones -- also something I consistently see missing from new analysts; - Only ~20% of buyside analysts do all of them consistently; - Retail investors? Almost none (lol) A thread 🧵: --- [2/14 @MapleLeafCap] What surprised me: The best pitches were often longer - but every word earned its place -- They didn't have "better access" (ok maybe sometimes) - they just asked better questions and proved their answers Result? Higher conviction, longer read-time, better returns. --- [3/14 @MapleLeafCap] 1/ Thesis conviction in the first paragraph Great pitches: 100% state their thesis definitively in the first 3 sentences Mediocre pitches: 67% contain hedging language like "tell me what I'm missing" The best analysts don't ask for permission. They state what they believe and why. --- [4/14 @MapleLeafCap] 2/ A clearly stated variant view Every great pitch answers: "What does the market believe, and why is it wrong?" Not "this is undervalued" - that's a conclusion, not an edge "Consensus thinks margins peak at 15%, but my channel checks show 22% is sustainable because..." - that's a variant view. --- [5/14 @MapleLeafCap] 3/ Proprietary primary research "3 former execs told me the product pipeline is stronger than reported" "Top 3 customers confirmed they're increasing spend 40%" "A competitor's sales rep said they're losing deals to this company" You can't find this in 10-Ks. The best pitches prove their edge with sources. --- [6/14 @MapleLeafCap] 4/ Scenario analysis that tells a story Not just bull/base/bear with numbers in a table The best pitches walk you through each world: "In the bull case, AWS reprices and margins expand to X because Y happens... here's exactly what that looks like..." Assumptions explicit. Logic clear. You can follow the math. --- [7/14 @MapleLeafCap] 5/ Specific risks with kill conditions Mediocre: "competition could increase" Elite: "if AWS cuts prices 20%, margins compress to X% - I exit at $Y" The best analysts define exactly what would prove them wrong. No ego. Just process. --- [8/14 @MapleLeafCap] 6/ No background padding Mediocre pitches: 2 pages of company history before the thesis Great pitches: just enough context for the decision - nothing more Background is what weak analysts hide behind. Your reader is busy. Respect their time. --- [9/14 @MapleLeafCap] 7/ Explicit downside floor with asymmetric framing The best pitches quantify both sides: "$2 of downside, $20+ of upside" "If I'm wrong, I lose 15%. If I'm right, I 3x." This isn't confidence theater - it's showing you did the work on the downside too. --- [10/14 @MapleLeafCap] The pattern? Great pitches are decision-ready. They give you: - Why the market is wrong (variant view) - Proprietary evidence backing it - Scenarios that tell a story, not just numbers - What would change their mind (kill conditions) - Only what matters Everything else is noise. --- [11/14 @MapleLeafCap] So I built an AI that writes pitches this way. 6 AI analysts with different investing philosophies debate each other across 5 rounds A research director challenges every assumption The output: institutional-quality memos in 30 minutes See examples: http://tickertothesis.com --- [12/14 @MapleLeafCap] Here are a few examples: --- [13/14 @MapleLeafCap] Want to try it yourself? I packaged the whole system as a downloadable skill you can run locally Go to http://bidclub.ai (@bidclubai) and grab it: https://www.bidclub.ai/post/eefb6740-2a94-4a0e-9149-17fa70f76d32 Generate your own buyside-quality research on any ticker --- [14/14 @MapleLeafCap] tl;dr - after analyzing 10,000+ analyst reports: 1. Lead with conviction 2. Prove your variant view 3. Cite proprietary sources 4. Tell stories with scenarios 5. Define your kill conditions 6. Cut the fluff 7. Show asymmetric payoff The market rewards clarity.
